name: FAIR Data
title: FAIR Data
answer: FAIR Data is a set of guiding principles for making research data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. It applies to datasets, metadata, code, and the repositories that hold them, not just to files on a disk. In practice it covers identifiers, rich descriptions, clear access conditions, standard vocabularies, and provenance records. The aim is to let people and machines discover and combine data across institutions and domains. For an AI researcher, FAIR data is the difference between a dataset that can be cited and reused and one that is effectively lost.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: FAIR Data is a set of guiding principles for making research data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. It applies to datasets, metadata, code, and the repositories that hold them, not just to files on a disk. In practice it covers identifiers, rich descriptions, clear access conditions, standard vocabularies, and provenance records. The aim is to let people and machines discover and combine data across institutions and domains. For an AI researcher, FAIR data is the difference between a dataset that can be cited and reused and one that is effectively lost.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: FAIR data runs on repository platforms, persistent identifier services, metadata schemas, and storage that can serve both humans and machines. Common building blocks include DOIs for datasets, ORCID iDs for people, DataCite metadata, and domain repositories that expose APIs and OAI-PMH endpoints. Institutional repositories, cloud object stores, and catalogues provide the underlying storage and search layers. Versioning systems and checksums help keep track of changes and verify integrity. The infrastructure is less a single product than a chain of services that must agree on identifiers and formats.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work of FAIR data starts with planning, then documenting, then depositing, then maintaining. Researchers create a data management plan, choose a repository, assign a persistent identifier, and write metadata that follows a community schema. They use controlled vocabularies and ontologies so that terms mean the same thing across datasets. They record provenance, licenses, and access conditions, and they link data to publications and code. Repository staff and data stewards often review the deposit to check that the metadata is complete and the files are usable.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in FAIR data turn on consent, licensing, privacy, and provenance. Accessible does not mean open to everyone, so sensitive data can be FAIR through controlled access and clear conditions. Licenses such as Creative Commons or community-specific agreements state what others may do with the data. Provenance records show where data came from and how it was processed, which matters for trust and for correcting errors. Repositories also carry responsibilities for preservation, takedown requests, and compliance with funder or institutional policies.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: FAIR data is moving toward machine-actionable metadata, automated provenance capture, and closer links between data, models, and publications. The FAIR principles are being extended to software, workflows, and AI training datasets, where documentation such as datasheets and model cards is becoming more common. Repositories are adding APIs and semantic search so that agents can query collections without human mediation. A library that holds 135 research papers and 13608 extracted claims shows how much value sits in structured links between sources and assertions. The next step is to make those links persistent, citable, and reusable across systems.
